title: What Audible Learned About 7,000 Listeners From Its NYC Bookless Bookstore: ‘How Do We Take Something Invisible and Make It Tangible?’
description: More than half of Americans aged 18 and older, an estimated 157 million people, have listened to an audiobook, according to the Audio Publishers Ass
body:
More than half of Americans aged 18 and older, an estimated 157 million people, have listened to an audiobook, according to the Audio Publishers Association. Back in May, Audible likely added a few more to the fold with its Story House experience, which the Amazon-owned audiobook company proclaimed to be the first ever “bookless bookstore.”

	Following a pop-up during the return of BookCon at NYC’s Javits Convention Center in April, the Audible Story House operated for a month (from May 1-May 31) in lower Manhattan and saw more than 7,000 unique visitors come through its free-to-enter doors.
	

	“What I was excited about was the opportunity to learn a lot more about customers and their experiences in that space,” Audible’s global head of brand content marketing James Finn tells Variety. “And oftentimes, I don’t have a sample size like that, and I don’t have a situation where we show up for an entire month in a city like New York and really learn more about our existing customers and new listeners.”




	

									Nick Castle
	



	Located at 260 Bowery, the three-floor audiobook space offered guests the chance to browse titles using physical “Story Tiles” (blocks with RFID chips that made listening to samples via speakers, headphones or through your own phone and earbuds a quick business) throughout seven distinct listening spaces. It housed an immersive listening theater with Dolby Atmos surround sound and a “Listening Bar” with a dedicated “Story Tender” staffer offering up personalized recommendations for sampling. There were creator programming and panels, book clubs, hands-on crafting activities, a pop-up cafe from Brooklyn’s Land to Sea and tons of merch.
	

	But come June, it was all gone.

	“It was very hard when we closed the doors, I will be honest,” Finn says. “And a lot of people assumed that it was going to be there permanently, which was a nice compliment to the team that built the space.”

	Out of the 301 titles that were on offer in Audible’s Story House (“We never say what the one title is because everybody had an opinion — but we wanted to add that one more,” Finn says) 98% of the audiobooks were listened to “to any degree” over the course of the month in operation. The most popular included “Project Hail Mary,” “The Hive: A Thriller,” “George Orwell’s 1984,” “Just Kiss Already,” and Audible’s full-cast recording of “Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone.” 



	

					Photo by Bryan Bedder/Getty Images for Audible
									Getty Images for Audible
	



	There was also a lot of interest in Matt Dinniman’s “Dungeon Crawler Carl” LitRPG series, which released new book, “A Parade of Horribles” on May 12. “People were coming in, and they had already listened to it, and the eighth book had only come out a couple days ahead of time, and they were still tapping it, and they still were excited about that,” Finn says.

	But it wasn’t just the “Carl” fans that were sticking around. Audible says it counted more than 15,000 “deep engagement” experiences among its Story House guests, meaning the person did more than simply enter the space and browse.

	“People weren’t just coming in and then leaving, or coming in and listening to a sample and leaving,” Finn says. “They genuinely were staying around, going to the different areas, or coming to the community sessions where we had different activities, or going up to the cafe and buying an AudiBuddy and that was really interesting.” 

	Finn says the Audible team has also been looking at “what are the learnings from the actual experience in New York that we can adapt to the experience within the app and within the service.” The biggest takeaway: “removing friction and allowing more engagement and allowing more of an opportunity for personalization, so that they have the opportunity to go to what’s interesting to them, but to sample and to try.”



	

					Audible
	



	Audible now has those 13,000 leftover “Story Tiles,” so there are some plans for what to do with those tactile representations of audiobooks.
	

	“We created that technology and that item. It didn’t exist,” Finn says. “The ambition was, how do we take something invisible and make it tangible? So the RFID component with it, we were able to see what people were listening to, and it was fantastic because everybody has different tastes and we saw such an interesting read across the entire slate of content there.”

	Finn adds: “But after the fact, what we’ve been doing is assessing what does Audible Story House look like in our plans for ’27. Right now, what we’re doing is similar to what you saw at BookCon. We’re going to bring a version of that with the core fundamentals to Guadalajara Book Festival, and then Frankfurt Book Fair.”

title: Oscars: 7 Films That Could Define the Awards Season, From ‘The Odyssey’ to ‘Michael’
description:
The frontrunners have a head start. The festivals have contenders ready to run them down. Let the games begin. 

	The film year has already delivere
body:
The frontrunners have a head start. The festivals have contenders ready to run them down. Let the games begin. 

	The film year has already delivered, led by Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” a July event picture that doubled as the first true best picture launch of 2026. Back in May, Cannes fired the opening shots, sending Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” Netflix-acquired Spanish-language epic “La Bola Negra” and Russian drama “Minotaur” down the Croisette with buzz that will trail them into the fall. 
	

	But a frontrunner in August is just a film with an earlier release date. Over the next six weeks, the Oscars race will unspool in waves — the thin air of Telluride, the carpets of Venice’s Lido, the crowds of Toronto, the tastemakers of New York — with a single afternoon screening able to rewrite the whole narrative.  


	The festivals are set, and the year is loaded. And a moonwalk, a Homeric voyage and a Pixar goodbye are all in play at the same time. Here’s where the race stands. 



	

					PROJECT HAIL MARY, Ryan Gosling, 2026. © Amazon MGM Studios /Courtesy Everett Collection
									©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		“Project Hail Mary” (Amazon MGM Studios) 	

	Ryan Gosling has three Oscar nominations — for “Half Nelson,” “La La Land” and “Barbie” — and no wins, and this adaptation of Andy Weir’s novel could hand him another shot. It also marks the live-action sci-fi leap of Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, the “Lego Movie” and “21 Jump Street” duo. Oscar history isn’t usually kind to directing partnerships: Only a handful have been nominated, most recently the Daniels for “Everything Everywhere All at Once.” Lord and Miller could join that short list, if Amazon MGM builds a friendly reminder campaign around them. 
	



	

	


	
		“The Odyssey” (Universal Pictures) 	

	No surprise, Nolan is the man to beat, and “The Odyssey” is exactly the kind of feat the Academy’s directors branch loves to reward. His adaptation of Homer’s epic arrived to a wave of critical love, the rare summer tentpole with awards ambition built into its foundation: mythic source material, a starry ensemble and a theatrical approach designed to make the format itself part of the conversation. Two years after the “Oppenheimer” sweep — his first directing Oscar and a best picture win shared with wife and producing partner Emma Thomas — Nolan enters this campaign with a lot of Academy goodwill. Matt Damon’s Odysseus could put him in serious play in the actor race after winning a screenwriting Oscar nearly 30 years ago for “Good Will Hunting.” At the same time, John Leguizamo, Robert Pattinson, Anne Hathaway and Samantha Morton crowd a supporting field. 



	

					Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson in Michael. Photo Credit: Courtesy of Lionsgate
									Courtesy of Lionsgate
	


	
		“Michael” (Lionsgate) 	

	Every season has an unofficial Oscar “villain” — think “Green Book,” “Bohemian Rhapsody” and “Emilia Pérez.” This year has a moonwalk. “Michael” doesn’t need critics (it has a 38% Rotten score, but a 97% Certified Fresh rating); it needs the Academy’s populist wing, the same bloc that widened best picture to 10 slots after the 2008 “Dark Knight” snub to make room for films the public embraced. Jaafar Jackson’s transformation into the King of Pop will be the main talking point, and two-time Oscar nominee Colman Domingo’s chilling turn as family patriarch Joe Jackson lends the film gravity. Factor in the craft branches — editing, sound and makeup and hairstyling — and voters have plenty of boxes to check. 



	

					Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penélope Cruz and Edward Norton appear in The Invite by Olivia Wilde, an official selection of the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Courtesy of Sundance Institute | photo c/o The Invite
									The Invite
	


	
		“The Invite” (A24) 	

	Olivia Wilde’s third feature is her sleekest, most assured work behind the camera, and A24 is mounting a full fall campaign. An English-language remake of Cesc Gay’s “The People Upstairs,” it boasts one of the year’s most impeccable ensembles: Seth Rogen, Wilde, four-time nominee Edward Norton and Oscar winner Penélope Cruz (a triple threat this year, with “La Bola Negra” and “Bunker” still to come). The engine is a crackling script by Rashida Jones and Will McCormack (reunited after “Celeste and Jesse Forever”) that offers sharp dialogue, a merciless structure and relentless laughs. In a season that rewards originals and adaptations alike, this is writing voters will likely remember in January and a cast the actors branch can get behind. 
	



	

					OBSESSION, Inde Navarrette, 2025. © Focus Features /Courtesy Everett Collection
									©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		“Obsession” (Focus Features) 	

	If “Get Out” had Daniel Kaluuya, “Obsession” has Inde Navarrette. The horror breakout — the highest-grossing film in Focus Features history — lives and dies by its star, who plays a hypnotized co-worker and love interest with fearless physicality. Destined to be one of the year’s signature discoveries, as proven by her casting as Rogue in the upcoming “X-Men” movie, Navarrette could emerge as a critics’ awards darling, and Focus has every reason to push hard — perhaps even for writer-director-editor Curry Barker and a best picture slot. 



	

					“I Swear”
									Graeme Hunter Pictures
	


	
		“I Swear” (Sony Pictures Classics)	

	The N-word outburst at the BAFTA Awards put “I Swear” in the headlines and buried the real story: Robert Aramayo deserved that surprise win for lead actor. As a man living with Tourette’s syndrome, the 33-year-old English actor delivered an invigorating, deeply human turn that topped Timothée Chalamet’s in “Marty Supreme” and Michael B. Jordan’s in “Sinners.” The film’s U.S. release date makes it eligible for the Golden Globes, Critics Choice and the Oscars. If enough voters see it, they’ll understand why Aramayo won the BAFTA — and the film could get other Oscar nominations, including original screenplay.



	

					TOY STORY 5, from left: Bullseye, Jessie (voice: Joan Cusack), 2026. © Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures / Courtesy Everett Collection
									©Walt Disney Co./Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		“Toy Story 5” (Pixar) 	

	“Toy Story 5” is a $1 billion juggernaut and the kind of overwhelming favorite the category bends around; Pixar sequels lock up nominations before the competition has finished storyboarding. The film also gets a boost from legendary composer Randy Newman and superstar Taylor Swift. The franchise carries a perfect Oscar record: All four previous “Toy Story” films earned best original song nominations, the only series with a flawless mark in the category. Pixar could extend the streak with “I Knew It, I Knew You,” written by Swift and Jack Antonoff — which would also hand Swift, a record four-time album of the year Grammy winner, her first Oscar bid after two near misses. In a franchise built on goodbyes, one more song may be all it takes.
	



	

					Jimmy Gonzales, Matt Damon and Himesh Patel in “The Odyssey”
									Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures

title: ‘Squid Game’ Star Lee Byung-hun, Creator Hwang Dong-hyuk Reunite for Thriller ‘K.O. Club’
description: Lee Byung-hun is reuniting with “Squid Game” creator Hwang Dong-hyuk on sci-fi thriller “K.O. Club,” the director’s first feature film in nearly a d
body:
Lee Byung-hun is reuniting with “Squid Game” creator Hwang Dong-hyuk on sci-fi thriller “K.O. Club,” the director’s first feature film in nearly a decade. 

	Firstman Studio, the production company Hwang runs with producer Kim Ji-yeon, confirmed the casting, with filming targeted for the first half of 2027.

	Lee, who played the Front Man across the “Squid Game” franchise, headlines a lineup that also includes fellow franchise alum Park Hae-soo. Rounding out the ensemble are Oh Jung-se (“It’s Okay to Not Be Okay”), Cho Yeo-jeong (“Parasite”) and Kim So-jin (“The Man Standing Next”), each working with Hwang for the first time.
	

	The film centers on a near-future in which wealth can buy biological youth, pitting an aging elite that hoards money and power against a younger generation locked out of both. “K.O. Club” is shorthand for “Killing Oldmen Club,” a title that spells out the class war at the story’s core.


	Firstman Studio built its reputation carrying “Squid Game” to a global audience and has since branched into television with the series “Affairs Not the Only Secret.” “K.O. Club” represents the company’s return to feature production alongside its founder.

	Hwang last released a theatrical film in 2017 with the historical drama “The Fortress,” following earlier credits including comedy “Miss Granny” and drama “Silenced.” He became the first Asian director honored with a directing Emmy for a foreign-language series on the strength of “Squid Game.”

	Lee’s recent credits include Park Chan-wook’s “No Other Choice” and the Go drama “The Match.”

	“Squid Game” ran for three seasons on Netflix and became one of the platform’s most-watched series worldwide, cementing Hwang as one of Korean entertainment’s most closely watched exports heading into his return to the big screen.

schema.headline: ‘Squid Game’ Star Lee Byung-hun, Creator Hwang Dong-hyuk Reunite for Thriller ‘K.O. Club’

title: Plans in Development to Replace Edinburgh TV Festival as it Moves to Manchester
description: Scotland’s screen bodies are working on a new Edinburgh-based festival for the media and creative industries as the TV Festival moves to Manchester.
body:
Scotland’s screen bodies are working on a new Edinburgh-based festival for the media and creative industries as the TV Festival moves to Manchester.

	Màiri McAllan Cabinet Secretary for Education, Culture and Gaelic confirmed the news at a launch event on the penultimate night of the festival. “Baby Reindeer” creator Richard Gadd was among the attendees at the event.

	Screen Scotland are developing the new event with an eye to integrating it with other creative festivals that run in the city throughout August, including the Edinburgh Fringe and Edinburgh International Film Festival. Consultant Rowan Woods has been appointed to explore the idea, funded by Screen Scotland and delivered through The Fringe Society. Woods will consult widely with various stakeholders – including the other festivals as well as venues, broadcasters and producers – to establish the scope and shape of the event.
	

	Consultation is expected to wrap in spring 2027 with a pilot planned for next summer.


	Screen Scotland has already confirmed it will establish a new debate format, titled the Lynda Myles Debate, as part of the offering, named for Lynda Myles, formerly director of the EIFF and co-creator of the Edinburgh TV Festival.

	“We are so proud of Scotland’s screen sector and this exciting addition to the August festivals line-up will provide a new way to embrace the creativity and cultural innovation which makes our capital unique,” said McAllan. “As a global hotbed of emerging talent, where new voices are heard and fresh stories are told, Edinburgh will continue its world-leading offer for the television industry with the support of the Scottish Government – and will do so alongside our other Edinburgh festivals, showcasing brilliance across artforms.”
	

	Earlier this year the TV Festival, which celebrates its fiftieth anniversary this year, confirmed it would be moving to Manchester from 2027.

schema.headline: Plans in Development to Replace Edinburgh TV Festival as it Moves to Manchester

title: This AncestryDNA Labor Day Sale Helps You ‘Find Your Roots’ at Home for a Portion of the Price
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	AncestryD
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	AncestryDNA is offering one of its steepest discounts of the year for Labor Day, giving amateur genealogists a cheaper way to uncover the kinds of family secrets that regularly leave celebrities stunned on PBS’ “Finding Your Roots.”

	Through Sept. 8 at 10 a.m. ET, the genealogy company is taking up to 75% off its DNA offers, dropping the standard AncestryDNA kit from $99 to $34. The test provides an ancestral origins report spanning more than 3,600 geographic regions, plus connections to genetic relatives in Ancestry’s database.
	

	For just one dollar more, the AncestryDNA + World Explorer Membership package is $35, down from $100, and bundles the DNA kit with three months of Ancestry’s World Explorer plan for $1. The membership unlocks the company’s collection of more than 70 billion U.S. and international records, along with DNA-by-parent tools and more than 100 DNA Traits. The subscription automatically renews at $99.95 every three months unless canceled. An All Access bundle, which adds Newspapers.com, Fold3 military records and accounts for up to five people, is also discounted from $199 to $44 and renews for $149 every three months.


	Ancestry has an especially close connection to the celebrity-genealogy boom: the company is a corporate sponsor of PBS’ “Finding Your Roots,” Henry Louis Gates Jr.’s long-running series that combines historical records with DNA analysis to reconstruct the family trees of actors, musicians, athletes and other notable guests. Ancestry has also turned the show into a major piece of its own entertainment marketing, hosting episode recaps and celebrity clips and encouraging viewers to use its DNA tests and record database to conduct a DIY version of the research seen on screen.
	

	Season 12, which aired earlier this year, included everyone from America Ferrera and Darren Criss to Lizzo, Flea, Spike Lee, Kristin Chenoweth, Brittney Griner and Chris Paul. Among its stranger revelations: Hasan Minhaj discovered evidence suggesting his family may have descended from royalty in northern India, while Lizzy Caplan learned that an ancestor arrived in New York with just $3 and that branches of the family she had thought of as Russian were actually rooted in Poland.

	The show has already lined up another star-heavy batch of genealogy guinea pigs. “Finding Your Roots” Season 13 is set to premiere Jan. 12, 2027, with guests including Bette Midler, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Rita Moreno, Noah Wyle, Carrie Coon, Elizabeth Banks, Nikki Glaser, Mark Cuban and Melissa Etheridge.

	That said, DNA companies have faced increasing scrutiny over what happens to genetic information once it enters a private database — an issue thrown into sharp relief by 23andMe’s bankruptcy in 2025. The company’s consumer-genetics assets, including its customer data, were ultimately acquired for $305 million by the nonprofit 23andMe Research Institute, formerly known as TTAM Research Institute and founded by 23andMe co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The transaction followed a 2023 security breach that compromised information connected to millions of customers and sparked renewed debate around the protection of genetic data.

	That turmoil arguably makes Ancestry’s current privacy structure a more reassuring proposition than 23andMe’s recent history, though no commercial DNA test is entirely without privacy considerations. Ancestry says it does not voluntarily give law enforcement access to customer data, requires valid legal process for government requests and prohibits law enforcement from using its service to investigate crimes or identify human remains. Users can also permanently delete their DNA results and separately request destruction of their physical biological sample. Genetic information is only included in research shared with outside partners when a user opts into Ancestry’s informed-consent program.

	Ancestry’s combination of a massive historical-record library, genetic matching and explicit deletion and law-enforcement policies makes it particularly well suited to people interested primarily in genealogy rather than health-risk testing.
	

	The AncestryDNA portion of the Labor Day sale runs through Sept. 8 at 10 a.m. ET.

schema.headline: This AncestryDNA Labor Day Sale Helps You ‘Find Your Roots’ at Home for a Portion of the Price

title: Director of Haugesund Closing Film ‘The Murder of Benjamin’ Says the Infamous Neo-Nazi Killing Was a ‘Wake-Up Call for the Whole Nation’ But ‘They Are Rising Again’
description:
Norwegian director Ingvild Søderlind says that the 2001 killing of Benjamin Hermansen was a “wake-up call for the whole nation.”

	Hermansen, a teen
body:
Norwegian director Ingvild Søderlind says that the 2001 killing of Benjamin Hermansen was a “wake-up call for the whole nation.”

	Hermansen, a teenager born to a Norwegian mother and a Ghanaian father, was stabbed to death by neo-Nazis. 

	“It was a tragic culmination of a wave of neo-Nazism in Norway in the ’90s. But it also resulted in a large anti-racism movement,” she recalls. Still, for the longest time, people were too scared of the film she wanted to make.
	

	“The Murder of Benjamin” is the closing  the 54th Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund.


	“So many said: ‘We don’t want to show the perpetrators.’ Because of that, it was very difficult to fund it – until I joined forces with producer Thomas Robsahm [of Nordisk Film Production]. Unfortunately, as we were making the film, we experienced that its theme was becoming increasingly relevant. They are rising again.”

	The team has already experienced hate following the release of the trailer. 

	“We had to remove some comments because they were so offensive,” she says. 

	“I expect some backlash and even sympathy for the perpetrators from some young people. But I also hope these debates will raise awareness of microaggressions and racism.”

	In “The Murder of Benjamin,” Søderlind follows multiple points of view: Those of Benjamin himself, his killers, and his mother, fighting for a fair trial. 

	Marit Hermansen, who passed away in 2019, became an activist after the tragedy. 

	“I met her. She became a known figure in Norway and a woman who spoke out against racism. She initiated several initiatives to encourage schools to prevent racist behavior.”
	

	“At first, she wasn’t supposed to play such a big part in this story. But the more I developed it, the more interested I became in her. I’m also white, so to take on a film that talks about these issues, I had to take on her perspective. In the film, she says to Benjamin: ‘I don’t know how it feels.’ And neither do I.”

	She’s played by Laila Goody alongside Elikem Leon Akpan, cast as Benjamin, and Magnús Blöndal Jóhannson as the boy responsible for his death. 

	“I wanted to show the perpetrator because he’s a typical example of someone who got into an extreme environment in search of shelter and safety. He’s well-known in Norway – he talked about his background in an interview with the national news,” says Søderlind.

	“Members of the Oslo neo-Nazi movement in the 90s announced themselves as ‘the protectors of the society.’ For me, it was important to make a film about being outside of the society. These three people all look for belonging.”

	She wanted to be “honest with the audience” about the story – starting from that unflinchingly direct title. 

	“I know it’s painful, but so is the film,” she states.

	“Benjamin was a Norwegian boy, regardless of the color of his skin. It was important to say this clearly and show him as a normal teenage Norwegian boy. We didn’t want to turn him into a saint. We wanted to show a normal life that has suddenly came to an end.”

	The film, sold by TrustNordisk, is finished. But Søderlind’s job isn’t quite done. 

	“My dream scenario would be for everyone to understand their personal responsibility in how they carry themselves through this world and how they treat other people. I’m going to show the film to many young people, also in schools, and we will have discussions afterwards.”

	“I’ve worked with kids before, including those from multicultural backgrounds, and I remember the stories they told me. The scene when the boys are stopped by the police? I met a lot of kids who experience this. The police basically tell them they’re ‘bad people’.”

	“Sometimes we say that words are harmless. They aren’t harmless.”

schema.headline: Director of Haugesund Closing Film ‘The Murder of Benjamin’ Says the Infamous Neo-Nazi Killing Was a ‘Wake-Up Call for the Whole Nation’ But ‘They Are Rising Again’

title: CNN Apologizes for Mistakenly Airing Photo of Dolly Parton Impersonator in Report on Late Singer
description: CNN has apologized to the family of Dolly Parton after the news network incorrectly showed a photo on the air of a Dolly Parton tribute artist inste
body:
CNN has apologized to the family of Dolly Parton after the news network incorrectly showed a photo on the air of a Dolly Parton tribute artist instead of the famed country singer herself.

	On Tuesday evening’s broadcast of CNN’s “Laura Coates Live” in the 11 p.m. ET hour, in a report about the death of Parton, the network displayed a photo that was actually of Kelly Vohnn, a Las Vegas performer who has portrayed Dolly Parton over the course of her career.
	

	In a statement to Variety, CNN said, “We regret the error and apologize to the Parton family.”


	The Getty Images photo of Vohnn used by CNN (above right) was taken Dec. 16, 2025, in Las Vegas, where Vohnn was attending a screening of the movie “Song Sung Blue” at Brenden Theatres inside the Palms Casino Resort, according to the photo agency. 

	In an interview with the New York Post, which first reported on CNN’s apology over the mix-up, Vohnn said, “I started getting all these texts in from friends saying that I was on CNN, and I couldn’t believe it.” She continued, “I was already heartbroken at losing Dolly because of how much she has given to me as a woman and an artist. But then to see these images of me on screen was just weird.”

	The photo of Vohnn appeared in a montage of images on “Laura Coates Live,” which featured five photos of the actual Dolly Parton.



	

	



	Parton died Tuesday, Aug. 25, at the age of 80. She died after a “brief battle with cancer,” according to her reps.

	Parton wrote and performed hundreds of songs over a career spanning seven decades. Her best-known song is “I Will Always Love You,” alongside other hits like “9 to 5,” “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “Here You Come Again.” She also recorded a secret song, currently buried in a time capsule at her Dollywood resort in Tennessee, that is set to be opened in 2045 (in time for Parton’s 100th birthday).

schema.headline: CNN Apologizes for Mistakenly Airing Photo of Dolly Parton Impersonator in Report on Late Singer

title: BBC Director-General Matt Brittin Says Its News Service Is ‘A Disinfectant for Misinformation’
description: Matt Brittin, the new director-general of the BBC, delivered an impressive performance during a charged Q&A at the Edinburgh TV Festival, where he a
body:
Matt Brittin, the new director-general of the BBC, delivered an impressive performance during a charged Q&A at the Edinburgh TV Festival, where he answered questions on topics ranging from AI to budget cuts to the corporation’s ongoing legal battle with Donald Trump.

	Brittin, a longtime Google executive, took on the BBC’s top job, described by many as a “poisoned chalice,” in May.


	During his Thursday session at the festival, the one-time Olympic rower sparred with former “Newsnight” presenter Kirsty Wark on stage before taking rapid-fire questions from an audience comprised of journalists, producers, students and even a disgruntled political candidate who’d stood against Nigel Farage and Count Binface in the recent Clacton by-election.
	

	Despite his tech background, Brittin ditched the Q&A function on the festival’s app in favor of roaming microphones in the audience, giving him a chance to speak directly with his interrogators.

	That seemingly minor decision tallied with his message (given in response to Wark’s question about the BBC developing more YouTube channels) that at the BBC, “We should be closer to the audience.”

	“I mean, obviously, in terms of the stories we tell and the impact we have on people’s lives, better understanding what concerns them, but we also need to go where they are. BBC News should be everywhere, in my view. Everywhere — because it’s a disinfectant for misinformation.”

	That’s despite the fact the corporate is currently in the middle of a lawsuit with President Trump over a “Panorama” documentary in which the President’s speech during the infamous Jan. 6 riots was misleadingly edited. Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit in Florida over the revelation, leading to the resignation of Brittin’s predecessor Tim Davie.
	

	“Obviously, the decision to vigorously defend ourselves in the Florida court is something that predates me,” the current DG said, “but I very much support it. I think it’s really important that we defend our integrity. We moved to dismiss the case on the grounds of jurisdiction — in that nobody in the U.S. actually saw the show with the bad edit, and it was a bad edit.”

	Before taking the job, Brittin spent six weeks touring the U.K. and visiting various arms of the sprawling corporation, which includes television, news, radio, podcasts and production, among other facets.

	And he was not afraid to be frank about some of the over-production he had already seen at the corporation, for example with video podcasts. “We do need to offer that, but we don’t necessarily need to have radio studios with incredibly expensive cameras and monitors in front of the presenters face,” he pointed out. “We can do it better at home [on cheaper equipment] than we can in some of our studios.”

	The observation earned a sarcastic response from Wark, who replied: “Wow, we’ll just come to your house then.”

	Inevitably, talk turned to the BBC’s funding model, which is currently dropping to critical levels, with increasing numbers of viewers opting out of paying the license fee – required in the U.K. for watching any live television on any network and any platform – as they turn to streaming on demand, whether via behemoths like Netflix and Disney+ or YouTube. Coupled with inflation, it has created a massive gap in the BBC’s budgets, which are funded via the license fee as it is not allowed to run adverts.

	In his alternative McTaggart speech, former BBC media editor Amol Rajan said he was leaving the corporation partly because of its funding deficit. “Firstly, I think whatever the funding model, the BBC has got a big opportunity to have more impact on the audience…” said Brittin. “Secondly, it depends on the charter and the funding settlements exactly how we do that.”

	When Variety asked about Brittin’s proposal for a household levy – effectively a tax across the U.K. to fund the BBC — he replied: “It’s for the government to decide based on this consultation. What I’m making the case for is that we need sufficient funding to fulfil the remit well.”
	

	Brittin also said that if the BBC were to be funded via a household levy, it would potentially be cheaper than the current license fee, which is £180 per year ($245).

	“You might be able to go from sort of £15 a month per household down to like £12.”

	The last question came from a young aspiring broadcaster, who asked Brittin how he intends to make the BBC feel relevant for rising talent.

	“Well, I definitely think the BBC shouldn’t be what it wants was,” he replied. “It should be what it should be for the future. We need to reinvent the BBC for tomorrow.”

	He went on to share what persuaded him to take on the director-general job, revealing that it was something he’d read about the BBC’s launch a hundred years ago and how it had reinvented itself over that time. ““At the inception, the pioneers had no idea what they were doing,” he said. “They invented broadcast radio and the content had mad, inaccessible operas alongside recipes, and they then scaled it up.”

	“They reinvented broadcast and recording technology so that they could go and cover the D-Day landings and on and on and on,” he continued. “So I think the BBC has this incredible pioneering spirit at its best, and I want the BBC at its best for the future.”

schema.headline: BBC Director-General Matt Brittin Says Its News Service Is ‘A Disinfectant for Misinformation’

title: Penn Badgley to Lead ‘Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone’ Series at Amazon
description: Amazon has greenlit a series adaptation of the Benjamin Stevenson novel “Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone” with Penn Badgley set for the lea
body:
Amazon has greenlit a series adaptation of the Benjamin Stevenson novel “Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone” with Penn Badgley set for the lead role. 

	Academy Award nominee David Hemingson (“The Holdovers,” “Kitchen Confidential”) is attached to adapt the murder mystery book and serve as showrunner and executive producer, Bruna Papandrea, Steve Hutensky, and Jeanne Snow of Made Up Stories will also executive produce. Badgley will executive produce in addition to starring, with Stevenson also executive producing. Fifth Season and Made Up Stories will co-produce. 
	

	“I’m thrilled to be partnered with Fifth Season and Made Up Stories in bringing Ben’s heartfelt and darkly hilarious whodunit to life,” Hemingson said. “And we are so lucky to have Penn as our lead. I can’t think of any actor better suited to bring Ern’s intensity, brilliance and hilariously dry sense of humor to life.”


	Described as darkly comedic, the logline for the series states:

	“Set deep in the dense mountains of Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, the series follows Ern Cunningham (Badgley), a mystery-writing expert who reluctantly attends a family reunion to welcome his brother Michael home from prison — the same brother Ern helped convict. When a frozen body appears and a snowstorm traps everyone inside, the deaths begin to mount. Everyone in his family has already killed someone – either by accident or otherwise.” 

	A limited series adaptation of the book was previously in development at HBO in 2022 with Made Up Stories and Fifth Season (then Endeavor Content) producing, though it ultimately did not go forward. 
	

	“We’re beyond excited to bring Ben’s sensational book to life in Dave Hemingson’s brilliant hands” said Papandrea and Hutensky. “We’ve found the perfect ‘Ern’ in Penn and it’s a dream to be making this series with our amazing partners Amazon MGM Studios and Fifth Season.”

	Badgley is no stranger to murder and intrigue in television. He previously starred as the killer Joe Goldberg in the hit Netflix series “You” for five seasons, with that show airing its final season in 2025. He also previously played a major role in the hit CW drama “Gossip Girl.” His other TV roles include “The Slap” and “The Young and the Restless.” In film, Badgley will star in the upcoming Amazon MGM Studios romcom “You Deserve Each Other” opposite Meghann Fahy. That film is also based on a book and is also produced by Fifth Season. Badgley has previously been in films like “Easy A” and “Margin Call.” 

	“I am blown away by the vision and enthusiasm everyone has for bringing this book, and Ernest Cunningham, to the screen,” said Stevenson. “Penn perfectly captures Ern’s clueyness and cleverness, and David has brought bags of wit and heart to the script. With the passion of Amazon MGM Studios, Bruna and Steve behind us we have an absolutely killer team, and I can’t wait to solve a murder with them!”

	“Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone” was originally published by Mariner Books in 2022 and was a bestseller in Australia in by Penguin Random House in 2021. It is the first in the Ernest Cunningham book series, followed by “Everyone on This Train Is a Suspect,” “Everyone This Christmas Has a Secret,” and “Everyone in This Bank Is a Thief.” Stevenson is currently writing the fifth book. 

	“’Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone’ is a brilliantly inventive series that subverts the murder mystery genre in the most unexpected and entertaining ways,” said Peter Friedlander, head of global television at Amazon MGM Studios. “Ben created a world that is darkly funny and wickedly clever. Paired with David’s sharp storytelling and Penn’s magnetic presence, and with our incredible partners at Fifth Seasom and Made Up Stories, this series is going to be something truly special for Prime Video.”

	This series also marks the latest Fifth Season-Made Up Stories project based on a book. The two companies have previosuly collaborated on shows like “The Good Daughter” at Paeocck, “Nine Perfect Strangers” at Hulu, “Anatomy of a Scandal” at Netflix, and “The Lost Flowers of Alice Hart” at Prime Video. 
	

	Badgley is repped by Brillstein Entertainment Partners, CAA, The Lede Company, and Hansen Jacobson. Hemingson is repped by 3 Arts, WME, and McKuin Frankel & Whitehead. Stevenson is repped by Intellectual Property Group & Curtis Brown Australia.

schema.headline: Penn Badgley to Lead ‘Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone’ Series at Amazon

									WWD
	

		
	
				The blistering heat sweeping Los Angeles on Tuesday night didn’t stop Hollywood from coming out to celebrate the opening of Mother’s first-ever stand-alone store in Beverly Hills.
The guest list included a mix of actors, musicians, influencers and fashionistas, including Brittany Snow, Dave Grohl, Ana Phillippe, Alexandra Shipp, Jasmine Tookes and Daphne Guinness.
Hosted by Mother founders Lela Becker and Tim Kaeding – they’ve nicknamed the store “The Big Boy – the evening feature pink margaritas, champagne and mini fried chicken sandwiches. The big photo opp of the night, in addition to people posing in the boutique’s vintage phone booth, was taking pics of cigarettes offered throughout the store on silver platters.
“Smoking really is back in L.A., isn’t it?” one party guest said as another tucked a cigarette behind his ear.
With the news of Dolly Parton’s death announced just hours before the soiree, DJ Mei Kwok paid tribute by spinning a remix of the late icon’s “Jolene.”
The festivities wrapped up with pizza from next-door neighbor Mulberry Street Pizzeria served from Mother’s vintage El Camino.

                          Don't Use My Nazi Praise Against Me!!!
body:
Kanye West to Judge
                          Don't Use My Nazi Praise Against Me!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 27, 2026
                            11:30 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Kanye West is making moves to stop a jury from hearing about his past antisemitic social media posts ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            In court docs TMZ obtained, Kanye argues his old posts should not be used as evidence against him in the case brought by Benjamin Provo, who claimed he was a victim of race-based discrimination when he was fired from Donda Academy for having dreadlocks. Kanye said the posts have nothing to do with the case at hand.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Kanye included a 919-page report consisting of the alleged social media posts Benjamin plans to use. One included a post from Ye's Instagram profile which shows a Nazi robe with the caption, "Outfit of the day."
      

            According to the docs, other tweets Benjamin apparently intends to use read, "I'm a Nazi. Lets see if yall give that money back. I love Hitler. Now what bitches" ... and "I used to f*** employees in my office.”
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, Benjamin sued Kanye, claiming he experienced discrimination and retaliation while working for the musician's school in 2021. He claimed Kanye and other managers treated the Black employees less favorably than the white employees. He said Kanye often yelled at Black employees, while not doing that with white employees.
      
    
            Benjamin believed Kanye targeted him due to his dreads. The suit also claimed Kanye banned books by Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and other prominent Black leaders.
      
    
            Kanye denied all claims of wrongdoing. The case is headed to trial later this year.

title: 'Transformers' Voice Actor Peter Cullen Dead at 85

body:
'Transformers' Peter Cullen
                          Voice of Optimus Prime Dead at 85
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 27, 2026
                            7:02 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 27, 2026
                                10:13 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
            Peter Cullen, famous for voicing Optimus Prime in the 'Transformers' franchise, is dead.
      
    
            The legendary voice actor's agent tells TMZ ... Peter died Wednesday at his Los Angeles home.
      
    
            The cause of death is unclear.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Peter's family tells TMZ ... "Peter Cullen passed away peacefully, surrounded by his loving family - and held in the hearts of his many friends and countless fans worldwide. His family asks that you honor his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember 'be strong enough to be gentle.'"
      

            Peter voiced Optimus Prime, the leader of the Autobots, in the original 1980s "Transformers" animated TV series ... and returned to the role in the Michael Bay film series.
      
    
            In the first "Transformers" movie, Peter gives an iconic speech as Optimus Prime in the final scene.
      
    
            Peter is also known for voicing Predator in the 1987 "Predator" film.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            He was Eeyore in 'Winnie The Pooh' and Monterey Jack in "Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers," plus KARR in "Knight Rider" ... and on and on.
      
    
            Peter was even the voice of Mario in the original "Donkey Kong" animated series way back in the 1980s.
      
    
            He was 85.
      
    
            RIP
